title: Chromosome Number and Structure: Aneuploidy and Rearrangements

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In the chromosome-changes rule, what do dose, context and balance each ask?
cards.back: Dose: what DNA was gained or lost. Context: what a breakpoint disrupted or joined. Balance: what chromosome combinations meiosis can pass on.
cards.quote: Dose asks what DNA was gained or lost; context asks what a breakpoint disrupted or joined; balance asks what chromosome combinations meiosis can pass on.

cards.front: Why is chromosome count alone an incomplete guide to a chromosome change?
cards.back: A cell can have 46 chromosomes and still carry extra chromosome 21 material, and a rearrangement can change a gene without changing total DNA.
cards.quote: a cell can have 46 chromosomes and extra chromosome 21 material, and a rearrangement can change a gene without changing total DNA.

cards.front: {{c1::Aneuploidy}} is the gain or loss of individual chromosomes, short of a whole set.
cards.quote: both forms of aneuploidy: the gain or loss of individual chromosomes, short of a whole set.
cards.section: From one missed separation to four gametes

cards.front: In the classical model of one nondisjunction error with otherwise normal divisions, what four products does a meiosis I error give, and what does a meiosis II error give?
cards.back: Meiosis I: two disomic (n + 1) and two nullisomic (n − 1) products. Meiosis II: one disomic, one nullisomic and two normal products.
cards.why: At meiosis I homologues fail to part, so both daughter cells are abnormal; at meiosis II only one of the two cells errs.
cards.quote: a meiosis II error leaves one of each plus two normal products.
cards.section: From one missed separation to four gametes

cards.front: Fertilized by a normal egg, a disomic sperm gives a {{c1::trisomic}} zygote (three copies), and a nullisomic sperm gives a monosomic zygote (one copy).
cards.quote: With a normal egg these give trisomic (three copies) and monosomic (one copy) zygotes, both forms of aneuploidy
cards.section: From one missed separation to four gametes

cards.front: In a model of 100 meiocytes followed for one chromosome, 8 err at meiosis I, 4 err at meiosis II and 88 divide normally, with all four products of each recovered. How many of the 400 products are disomic, and what percent of zygotes with normal partners are trisomic?
cards.back: Meiosis I errors: 8 × 2 = 16 disomic. Meiosis II errors: 4 × 1 = 4. Total 20 of 400 disomic, so 5 percent of zygotes are trisomic (and 5 percent monosomic).
cards.quote: With normal partners, that would give 10 percent trisomic, 10 percent monosomic and 80 percent euploid (normal-number) zygotes.
cards.section: From one missed separation to four gametes

cards.front: Why does a DNA marker tightly linked to the centromere help tell a meiosis I error from a meiosis II error?
cards.back: Homologues near the centromere can carry different alleles, while sister copies usually match. Unless a crossover occurs between marker and centromere, two different alleles from one parent point to meiosis I; two copies of one allele point to meiosis II.
cards.quote: Near the centromere, homologues can carry different alleles, while sister copies usually match.

cards.front: A centromere-linked marker has alleles 1 and 2 in the father and 3 and 4 in the mother. A child with trisomy 21 has marker alleles 1, 3 and 4. Assuming no crossover between marker and centromere, which parent supplied the extra chromosome, and which classical division failed?
cards.back: The mother, at meiosis I. Alleles 3 and 4 came from both maternal homologues, which stayed together only if the homologues failed to separate.
cards.quote: The two different maternal alleles, 3 and 4, came from both maternal homologues, so the extra chromosome is maternal and the pattern points to maternal meiosis I.

cards.front: Same marker: alleles 1 and 2 in the father, 3 and 4 in the mother. A child with trisomy 21 has marker alleles 2, 2 and 3, and there is no crossover between marker and centromere. Which parent and which division?
cards.back: The father, at meiosis II. Two copies of the same paternal allele are sister copies, so the sisters failed to separate at the second division.
cards.quote: By contrast, a child with 1, 3 and 3 has two copies of one maternal allele, consistent with maternal meiosis II.

cards.front: Why can marker studies misassign a meiosis II error as meiosis I, and how is that risk reduced?
cards.back: A crossover between the marker and the centromere can make sister copies differ at the marker. Using markers as close to the centromere as possible reduces the risk.
cards.quote: a crossover between marker and centromere can make sisters differ at the marker, so a meiosis II error can resemble meiosis I, and the reverse.

cards.front: Which autosomal trisomies are seen regularly at birth in humans, and which is the commonest?
cards.back: Trisomies 21, 18 and 13; trisomy 21 is by far the commonest.
cards.quote: Of the autosomal trisomies only 21, 18 and 13 are seen regularly at birth, and trisomy 21 is by far the commonest.

cards.front: In family marker studies of free trisomy 21, which parent and which division most often explain the extra chromosome?
cards.back: Most free trisomy 21 is maternal in origin, and most maternal errors arise at meiosis I.
cards.quote: family marker studies found that most free trisomy 21 is maternal in origin and that most maternal errors arise at meiosis I.

cards.front: Turner syndrome occurs in females. What karyotype do about half of patients have, and what accounts for the rest?
cards.back: About half are 45,X (monosomy X). The rest have mosaicism (a mix of cell lines), a partly lost X or a rearranged X.
cards.quote: about half have monosomy X, a 45,X karyotype, while the rest have mosaicism (a mix of cell lines), a partly lost X or a rearranged X.

cards.front: {{c1::Klinefelter syndrome}} is most often 47,XXY, a male with an extra X, not 47,XYY.
cards.quote: Klinefelter syndrome is most often 47,XXY, a male with an extra X, not 47,XYY.

cards.front: The X chromosome is larger and carries more genes than chromosome 21. Why is an extra X usually better tolerated than an extra 21?
cards.back: Typical mammalian body cells largely inactivate each X beyond one, so an extra X adds much less active dose than its size suggests.
cards.quote: typical mammalian body cells largely inactivate each X beyond one, so an extra X adds much less active dose than its size suggests.

cards.front: If extra X chromosomes are largely inactivated, what is thought to explain the features that remain in 47,XXY and 45,X?
cards.back: Extra or missing active copies of the genes that escape X inactivation.
cards.quote: Extra or missing active copies of the genes that escape X inactivation are thought to explain many remaining features of 47,XXY and 45,X.

cards.front: A person has 47,XXX. Using the rule for extra X chromosomes, should the active X-gene dose rise by half compared with 46,XX? Give the reasoning.
cards.back: No, it should rise much less. Each X beyond one is largely inactivated, so the third X adds little active dose; genes that escape inactivation are thought to account for the remaining dose.
cards.quote: so an extra X adds much less active dose than its size suggests

cards.front: A {{c1::polyploid}} has complete extra chromosome sets.
cards.quote: A polyploid has complete extra chromosome sets.

cards.front: How does an autopolyploid differ from an allopolyploid, and how does each usually arise?
cards.back: An autopolyploid has extra sets from one species, often after a gamete fails to reduce its number. An allopolyploid combines sets from two or more species, usually after hybridization and chromosome-set doubling.
cards.quote: An autopolyploid has extra sets from one species, often after a gamete fails to reduce its chromosome number.

cards.front: Hexaploid bread wheat has 42 chromosomes in six sets from three ancestral grasses. Why does meiosis still form ordinary pairs?
cards.back: Each ancestral set has a partner, and genes such as Ph1 limit pairing with close relatives from the other ancestral sets.
cards.quote: Genes such as Ph1 limit pairing with close relatives from the other ancestral sets, so meiosis forms ordinary pairs.

cards.front: Why do triploid plants such as seedless bananas rarely form seeds, while wheat with six sets can make balanced gametes?
cards.back: Three matching sets cannot split evenly at meiosis, so nearly every triploid gamete is unbalanced. Wheat's sets each have a partner, so they form balanced pairs.
cards.why: Pairing, not dose alone, decides whether gametes come out balanced.
cards.quote: Three matching sets cannot split evenly at meiosis, so nearly every triploid gamete is unbalanced.

cards.front: What is the fate of human triploidy (69 chromosomes)?
cards.back: It is almost always lost during pregnancy.
cards.quote: Human triploidy, with 69 chromosomes, is almost always lost during pregnancy.

cards.front: Why is polyploidy common in flowering plants but rare in animals?
cards.back: Plants often self-fertilize or spread without sex, so a new polyploid need not find a matching partner, and they appear to tolerate dose shifts more readily.
cards.quote: Plants often self-fertilize or spread without sex, so a new polyploid need not find a matching partner, and they appear to tolerate dose shifts more readily.

cards.front: Loss of part of which chromosome arm causes cri du chat syndrome?
cards.back: The short arm of chromosome 5.
cards.quote: Loss of part of chromosome 5's short arm causes cri du chat syndrome.

cards.front: A {{c1::pericentric}} inversion includes the centromere; a paracentric inversion does not.
cards.quote: A pericentric inversion includes the centromere; a paracentric inversion does not.

cards.front: In a heterozygote for a paracentric inversion, what do the two recombinant chromatids become after one crossover inside the loop?
cards.back: One dicentric chromatid, which breaks at anaphase, and one acentric fragment, which is lost.
cards.why: The inverted segment excludes the centromere, so the crossover joins two centromeres on one chromatid and leaves the other with none.
cards.quote: One crossover inside a paracentric loop produces one dicentric chromatid (two centromeres), which breaks at anaphase, and one acentric fragment (no centromere), which is lost.

cards.front: In a heterozygote for a pericentric inversion, what do the two recombinant chromatids carry after one crossover inside the loop?
cards.back: Each carries a duplication and a deletion, so both are unbalanced.
cards.quote: One crossover inside a pericentric loop gives two chromatids, each carrying a duplication and a deletion.

cards.front: An inversion heterozygote has a crossover within the inverted region in many meiocytes. Why do few recombinant offspring appear?
cards.back: The recombinant chromatids are unbalanced (a dicentric and acentric pair for paracentric, duplication plus deletion for pericentric), so the gametes rarely give viable offspring.
cards.quote: Either way the recombinant gametes are unbalanced, so few recombinants appear among offspring.

cards.front: A {{c1::Robertsonian translocation}} is a fusion, not a swap of ends: it joins the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes and loses most of their tiny short arms.
cards.quote: it joins the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes, whose centromere sits near one end, and loses most of their tiny short arms.

cards.front: Which human chromosomes are acrocentric?
cards.quote: In humans the acrocentrics are 13, 14, 15, 21 and 22.

cards.front: Why can a carrier of a Robertsonian translocation have 45 chromosomes and usually be unaffected?
cards.back: The lost short arms carry repeated ribosomal RNA genes, and the remaining acrocentrics retain many rRNA-gene copies. The long arms are still present in two doses.
cards.quote: Those short arms carry repeated ribosomal RNA genes and other repetitive DNA; the remaining acrocentrics retain many rRNA-gene copies.

cards.front: How can a child have Down syndrome with 46 chromosomes?
cards.back: A fusion chromosome carrying chromosome 21 material travels with a free 21 (translocation Down syndrome), so the child has three doses of 21 long-arm material in 46 chromosomes.
cards.quote: If a fusion carrying chromosome 21 material travels with a free 21, the child can have translocation Down syndrome with 46 chromosomes.

cards.front: What is the Philadelphia chromosome, and what does the exchange that makes it create?
cards.back: The small chromosome 22 left by an acquired 9;22 reciprocal translocation in blood cells. It joins BCR and ABL, and the fusion protein is a tyrosine kinase that stays switched on.
cards.quote: It is the small chromosome 22 left by an acquired 9;22 exchange in blood cells.

cards.front: Why does the Philadelphia chromosome show that disease can arise without net gain or loss of DNA?
cards.back: The critical change is gene context, not simply total dose: the exchange joins two genes into a fusion that acts abnormally.
cards.quote: Here the critical change is gene context, not simply total dose.

cards.front: What does a G-banded karyotype directly show?
cards.back: The chromosome count and band patterns, including balanced rearrangements; it sees only changes of roughly 5 to 10 million base pairs or larger.
cards.quote: A G-banded karyotype counts chromosomes and compares their band patterns.
cards.section: Choose a test by the question

cards.front: What is the main strength and the main limit of FISH?
cards.back: It uses a fluorescent probe for one chosen region and works in nondividing nuclei, but says nothing about regions outside its target.
cards.quote: It works in nondividing nuclei, but says nothing about regions outside its target.
cards.section: Choose a test by the question

cards.front: What does a chromosomal microarray measure, and what kinds of change is it blind to?
cards.back: It measures segment dose across the genome. It is blind to balanced changes, and a dose-only array can miss triploidy.
cards.quote: It is blind to balanced changes, and a dose-only array can miss triploidy.
cards.section: Choose a test by the question

cards.front: A child's banded karyotype looks normal, yet a dose-only microarray finds a small loss on one chromosome. Why could the karyotype miss it, and what could the array itself still miss?
cards.back: The loss is below the karyotype's routine resolution, while the array reads dose finely where probes are dense. The array would still miss a balanced rearrangement, because no dose changes.
cards.quote: The loss is below the karyotype's routine resolution; the array reads dose far more finely where probes are dense.
cards.section: Choose a test by the question

cards.front: A child has an unexplained loss of about 1 million base pairs somewhere in the genome. Among karyotype, FISH and chromosomal microarray, which first test fits, and why not the other two?
cards.back: Microarray. It reads dose genome-wide, where probes are dense down to tens of thousands of base pairs, depending on array and region. The karyotype sees only about 5 to 10 million base pairs or larger, and FISH checks only the region its probe targets.
cards.quote: Where probes are dense, it can find gains and losses down to tens of thousands of base pairs, depending on array and region.
cards.section: Choose a test by the question

cards.front: Banded karyotypes of leukaemia cells show a small chromosome 22 and extra stained material at the end of the long arm of one chromosome 9, about the size 22 has lost. A dose-only microarray shows no loss or gain on either chromosome. Which interpretation fits both results?
cards.back: A balanced reciprocal exchange of segments between 9 and 22. Banding shows material moved from 22 to 9, and the flat microarray shows no net dose change.
cards.quote: It is the routine genome-wide test that directly shows balanced rearrangements, but sees only changes of roughly 5 to 10 million base pairs or larger
cards.section: Choose a test by the question

cards.front: A man with typical features has 45 chromosomes, including a Robertsonian 14;21 translocation, and a child with Down syndrome. Why is he unaffected, which gametes make a normal-egg zygote that can survive, and how would you confirm the explanation?
cards.back: He has two doses of the long arms of 14 and 21, one free and one fused. Gametes expected to survive: 14 + 21 (normal), t(14;21) (balanced carrier), t(14;21) + 21 (translocation trisomy 21). The others (monosomy 21, trisomy 14, monosomy 14) are expected to be lost early. Karyotype the child and both parents; FISH for 21 can confirm the extra dose.
cards.quote: He has two doses of the long arms of 14 and 21, one free and one fused

cards.front: A Robertsonian 14;21 carrier makes six equally frequent gamete types in the usual 2:1 split. Only the normal, balanced-carrier and translocation-trisomy-21 zygotes survive with a normal egg. What fraction of liveborn children would have Down syndrome, and why are observed risks lower?
cards.back: 1 of 3 survivors, one in three. Observed risks are well below this conditional value, and lower when the father is the carrier than when the mother is.
cards.quote: If all six gametes were equally frequent and only types 1, 2 and 3 survived, one in three liveborn children would have Down syndrome.

cards.front: In human eggs, sister chromatids can separate early at meiosis I; in {{c1::reverse segregation}}, both pairs of sisters split at meiosis I.
cards.quote: In reverse segregation, both pairs of sisters split at meiosis I.
